newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Navigation freedom in South China Sea critical-U.S.
newsitem.headline: Navigation freedom in South China Sea critical-U.S.

text.p: The commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific said on Wednesday it was critical to keep freedom of navigation in the South China Sea in the face of disputes over ownership of islands in the area.

Admiral Joseph Prueher pledged the United States would abide by its obligations to the Philippines under their mutual defence treaty, but did not specifically say what Washington would do in case of an armed conflict over the disputed Spratly islands.

"The issue of freedom of navigation in the Spratlys and the use of the South China Sea overall is critical and we, through the MDB (Mutual Defence Board), will continue to work together with the Philippines on the Spratlys issue," he told a news conference.
"The Philippines can completely count on the fact that the United States will support all of its treaty obligations with the Philippines," he said.
Prueher was replying to a question on whether Manila could depend on U.S. assistance in case of an armed conflict in the South China Sea, which is one of the world's key waterways.
U.S. diplomats have said the U.S. treaty commitments do not cover disputed territories.
The Spratlys are a cluster of potentially oil-rich islets, reefs and atolls claimed wholly or in part by China, Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
A diplomatic row erupted between China and the Philippines in April when Manila accused Beijing of sending armed naval ships near two of the islands, which Manila claims.
Beijing, in turn, accused Manila of violating Chinese sovereignty after Filipinos hoisted their country's flag over a rocky outcrop called Scarborough Shoal north of the Spratlys.

Prueher headed the U.S. panel that met with Philippine military leaders -- led by armed forces chief General Arnulfo Acedera -- as part of the two countries' yearly MDB talks to discuss strengthening their security alliance.
Prueher said the board discussed the Spratlys dispute and that Washington wanted the Spratlys row settled peacefully.
An average of about 400 ships pass daily through the South China Sea.

Prueher said resumption of joint military exercises between the Philippines and the United States would depend on how soon they resolve the issue of jurisdiction over offences committed by U.S. servicemen while on Philippine soil.
The two countries last held joint exercises in 1995.
The United States maintained a military presence in its former colony for 98 years until it closed down Subic naval base in 1992 after Manila rejected a new bases treaty with Washington.
